1. Inspect the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems before work starts.
2. Inspect again as needed during the shift.
3. Inspect after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event.
4. Remove workers if you see cave-in signs, protective system failure, or a hazardous atmosphere.
5. Monitor water removal equipment and inspect runoff-prone excavations (1926.651(h)).
6. Decide what protection the trench gets; it is required at 5 ft or deeper.
- Your competent person decides on site.

There is no limit on the number of cans; the limits are 8 gallons per can and 200 pounds (440 lb) gross weight for everything on the truck together. Stay inside both and you need no placards or shipping papers under the materials of trade rule, 49 CFR 173.6 [1].

- Each gasoline can: no more than "30 L (8 gallons)" [1].
- All materials of trade on the truck combined (fuel, oil, spray paint and the like): no more than "200 kg (440 pounds)" gross weight [1]. Gasoline weighs about 6 lb per gallon, so the weight limit usually decides it before the can count does. A full 5-gallon can with its container is roughly 35 lb or more, which puts you around 12 cans, and that is before anything else on the truck.
- Cans must be metal or plastic safety cans, closed, secured and marked "gasoline". The driver must be told the hazardous material is on board [1].
- Diesel in non-bulk containers can be treated as a combustible liquid, and the hazmat rules then don't apply. A large diesel transfer tank is bulk packaging with its own marking and placard rules, so check the tank size before you buy one [1].

This is the federal rule. A company policy or a state rule can be stricter.

Call 911 now. Confusion and stumbling in the heat is treated as heat stroke (a medical emergency).

1. Call 911 (or your site's emergency number) and stay with him.
2. Move him to shade or an air-conditioned truck cab, out of the trench if it's safe.
3. Strip outer clothing and heavy gear, and soak his skin and clothes with cool water.
4. Put ice or cold wet towels on the head, neck, armpits and groin, and fan hard. Cold water immersion is best if you can set it up.
5. Keep cooling until EMS takes over, and give no fluids while he's confused.
6. If he stops breathing, start CPR.
